articles.summary: There's something primordially satisfying about watching a big-screen dinosaur get the what-for from the business end of a just-loaded shotgun. The recent run of Jurassic Park movies sometimes seems to have lost this primal pleasure, replacing it with ho-hum computer-generated spectacle and cheap nostalgic callbacks to the franchise's better days. They've forgotten that the franchise was founded on a combination of awe and white-knuckle terror—the raw and relatable fear of a giant, toothy monster that stalks the earth with a sort of evolutionary arrogance that comes from a couple million years atop the food chain. Newsflash: Humans rule the planet now. It's fun to watch these ancient planetary powerhouses get taken down a peg. Sic semper Tyrannosaurus. The End of Oak Street remembers what the Jurassic Park franchise has largely forgotten. It leans into the animal terror of encountering a dinosaur on the streets of an ordinary suburb. articles.author: Virginia Kruta
articles.summary: President Donald Trump turned a long-running joke into a birthday gift for Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who turned 55 on May 28. Trump has already tasked Rubio with several official jobs within the administration — which spawned constant speculation whenever a new vacancy appeared — and a viral meme was born. An Oval Office photo of Rubio slouched on a couch — wearing an expression that suggests he’s not thrilled with the way things are going — became the template for hundreds of potential new jobs for the Secretary of State/Acting National Security Adviser/acting administrator for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID)/acting archivist of the National Archives and Records Administration. Trump and other White House staffers capitalized on the popularity of the meme, and put together a collage — featuring dozens of iterations of the “Rubio realizing” meme. The finished product was framed in gold and presented to Rubio for his birthday.
